```{r setup}
library(cyclingpower)
```

Normalised power weights hard efforts more heavily than a plain average does,
so a given pair of average and normalised power implies something about how
ragged the ride was. `simulate_power()` inverts the usual calculation: instead
of summarising a ride you already rode, it builds a second-by-second series
that would produce the numbers you name.

```{r simulate}
ride <- withr::with_seed(1, simulate_power(3600, target_ap = 180, target_np = 220))

c(average_power = average_power(ride), normalised_power = normalised_power(ride))
```

Both targets are hit exactly rather than approximately, which is worth
explaining, because the obvious way to do this does not work well.

## Why not just optimise for it?

Asking an optimiser to choose all 3,600 values so that two summary statistics
come out right is a badly posed problem: 3,600 unknowns, two constraints, and
so infinitely many answers. It is also slow, and it lands on whichever solution
happens to sit nearest wherever the search began.

The deeper trouble is that a search starting from independent random values has
almost nothing to work with. Normalised power is defined on a thirty-second
rolling mean, and independent noise averages away inside that window, so a
series of random draws has a variability index of essentially 1 however wide
its spread.

```{r noise}
noise <- withr::with_seed(1, stats::rpois(3600, 200))
variability_index(noise)
```

Scatter alone cannot lift normalised power above the average. What lifts it is
sustained effort — holding 300 watts for two minutes, not flickering between 50
and 550 from one second to the next.

## Shape first, then scale

So the shape comes from an autocorrelated process, which is what riding
actually looks like, and the two targets are then met in a way that needs no
search over the ride at all.

Both metrics scale linearly with power, so their ratio is unaffected by the
overall level. That splits the problem cleanly in two. Raising the series to a
power stretches its peaks relative to its troughs and so sets the variability
index, `target_np / target_ap`; multiplying through afterwards sets the average
without disturbing the ratio. One monotone equation in one unknown, solved to
machine precision, rather than a search over every second.

The result is a ride you could plausibly have done, rather than an arbitrary
point in a very large solution space.

```{r trace}
plot(
  ride,
  type = "l",
  col = "grey60",
  main = "Simulated ride: AP 180 W, NP 220 W",
  xlab = "Seconds",
  ylab = "Power (W)"
)
lines(zoo::rollmean(ride, 30, fill = NA), col = "#0072B2", lwd = 2)
```

The distribution behind that trace is skewed: a long stretch of moderate power
with occasional hard efforts, which is what pulls normalised power forty watts
clear of the average.

```{r histogram}
hist(
  ride,
  breaks = 100,
  main = "Power distribution giving NP = 220, AP = 180",
  xlab = "Power (W)",
  ylab = "Frequency (seconds)"
)
```

## Controlling the character of the session

`smoothness` sets how long efforts are held. It does not change the statistics
— both rides below hit the same average and normalised power — but it changes
the session those statistics describe, from a punchy ride with frequent
surges to a few long sustained blocks.

```{r smoothness, fig.height = 5}
punchy <- withr::with_seed(3, simulate_power(1800, 180, 220, smoothness = 0.90))
sustained <- withr::with_seed(3, simulate_power(1800, 180, 220, smoothness = 0.995))

par(mfrow = c(2, 1), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
plot(punchy, type = "l", col = "grey50", main = "smoothness = 0.90",
     xlab = "", ylab = "Power (W)")
plot(sustained, type = "l", col = "grey50", main = "smoothness = 0.995",
     xlab = "Seconds", ylab = "Power (W)")
```

## What the targets do not pin down

Two numbers do not make a ride, and it is worth knowing where the series stops
being one. Nothing here knows about critical power, so a normalised power you
could not hold for an hour comes back as a series that would exhaust anyone —
but that is the target being impossible, not the simulation misbehaving. A
steady hour at the same normalised power would fail the same test.

Within a feasible intensity the shape is reasonable, but the tail underneath is
lognormal and widens as the variability index rises. The sustained peaks grow
with it, and they grow out of proportion to each other:

```{r peaks}
peak_over <- function(ride, window) {
  max(zoo::rollmean(ride, window, align = "right"))
}

vapply(c(steady = 190, ragged = 250), function(np) {
  ride <- withr::with_seed(1, simulate_power(3600, 180, np))
  c(`best 30s` = peak_over(ride, 30), `best 5min` = peak_over(ride, 300))
}, numeric(2))
```

A ragged ride posts a thirty-second best far above anything its five-minute
best would imply — not a power–duration curve any rider has. So read a high
variability index as the point where the output is still a series with the
right two numbers but no longer a plausible session.

Asking for a normalised power below the average is refused, since no series has
a variability index under 1. Asking for a very high one alongside a low
smoothness can also fail, because short surges cannot lift a thirty-second
average far; the error says so and suggests raising `smoothness`.
